transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Gonzalez (Quantum Payments EM), Liam O'Connor (Lead BE), Priya Singh (Security)

Summary: quick SDK walkthrough (Python + TypeScript), auth patterns (API key, service accounts, SSO), env setup, quickstarts and pilot/benchmark next steps. Security/compliance questions re: KMS, audit logs, private deployment.

Topics: SDK install, auth env vars, example quickstarts (text gen, streaming, embeddings), retries/timeouts, test harness for latency, security and dedicated capacity.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Avery from Redwood, I'll kick us off, and Samir who's our solutions engineer is here to walk through the SDKs and some examples. Maya, Liam, Priya, thanks for your time.
[00:12] Maya: Thanks, yeah keen to see how fast we can get a POC up. We're mostly Node/Python backend, critical to get auth and env setup right.
[00:22] Samir: Great. Agenda: quick install, auth options, live code snippets for Python and TypeScript, talk about env vars and local dev, then security notes and pilot/benchmark. We'll keep this interactive.
[00:33] Liam: Perfect. latency and cost are top of mind for us. We run payment flows, so 99th percentile tail latency matters.
[00:42] Samir: Understood. Redwood gives you a few levers — model choice, batching, prefix caching (we sometimes see docs call it KV "cash" in transcriptions), and dedicated pools. We'll demo SDK-level controls for timeouts/retries and streaming.
[00:55] Samir: First, install. Python: pip install redwood-inference (or pip install redwood-sdk is our short package depending on the repo) ; Node: npm install @redwood/inference.
[01:06] Maya: Any differences in features between the two SDKs?
[01:09] Samir: Feature parity for core API: generation, chat, embeddings, reranking, streaming and function/tool calling. Small divergences on helpers; we keep parity but sometimes TS has extra types, Python has convenience sync wrappers.
[01:22] Samir: Auth — three common patterns: 1) API key for hosted quickstarts 2) service accounts for CI/servers with scoped keys 3) SSO/OIDC for users and enterprise SAML for team provisioning. For private deployments you can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping.
[01:38] Samir: Example env vars we recommend: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_REGION (like us-east-1), REDWOOD_ENV (hosted|dedicated|private). For service accounts we add REDWOOD_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID and use short-lived tokens.
[01:50] Avery: we'll link the quickstart repo and an example .env file.
[01:54] [Shared link posted in chat: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts (repo: python, typescript, infra samples)]
[02:03] Samir: Live snippet — Python sync usage: 
    from redwood import RedwoodClient
    client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
    resp = client.generate(model='redwood-2-small', prompt='Summarize payment flow for merchant X')
    print(resp.text)

[02:26] Samir: And async/python streaming example: 
    async for chunk in client.stream_generate(...):
        process(chunk)

[02:35] Liam: How are streaming chunks delivered? Websocket? SSE?
[02:38] Samir: We support HTTP chunked streaming (EventStream/SSE-ish) and websocket for long-running sessions. In Node SDK you can attach a callback or use async iterator. The important bit: configure a read timeout and reconnect semantics in the SDK.
[02:50] Maya: For TypeScript can you show a quick example?
[02:53] Samir: Sure. TS quick example: 
    import Redwood from '@redwood/inference';
    const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
    const res = await client.text.generate({ model: 'redwood-2-small', input: '...' });

[03:10] Samir: For embeddings: 
    emb = client.embeddings.create({model: 'r-embed-uni-1', input: ['txn payload 1','txn payload 2']})

[03:19] Priya: Storage of embeddings — are those sent to Redwood and persisted? We need to know retention and encryption.
[03:25] Samir: By default hosted ingestion may cache or persist for quality improvements depending on customer agreement. For enterprise/dedicated you can opt out; with private you control storage. Everything's encrypted at rest; for BYOK we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping. We'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 cert.
[03:42] Maya: For local dev, what's the recommended pattern so engineers don't accidentally commit keys?
[03:46] Samir: Use .env with REDWOOD_API_KEY and add .env to .gitignore. For CI use secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, or Vault). We provide a small CLI helper to mint scoped tokens for short-lived jobs.
[03:58] Liam: Do you support IP allowlists or VPC egress restrictions?
[04:02] Samir: Yes — for dedicated and private we support VPC peering, customer-managed networking, and IP allowlists for hosted endpoints. We'll include the network architecture doc.
[04:12] [00:04:12] Maya: Ok, can you walk through error handling? We need graceful fallbacks — can't block a payment flow.
[04:18] Samir: Good point. Patterns: 1) client-side timeouts — set token generation timeout to, say, 200 ms for sync paths; 2) automatic retries with exponential backoff for idempotent calls; 3) fallback to smaller model or cached response; 4) circuit breaker at the application layer. Our SDK exposes retry_count, timeout_ms and a fallback hook where you can plug your own policy.
[04:38] Samir: Example config in TS: 
    const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: K, timeoutMs: 3000, retries: 2, fallback: (err) => cachedResponse });

[04:48] Liam: For the pilot we want to run a 5k qps simulated test to see latency and cost. What do you provide to help us?
[04:55] Samir: We'll provide a benchmark script in the quickstarts repo that can run against hosted and dedicated endpoints. It exercises both short chat and streaming. Also a sample tracing hook to push traces into your observability. We'll work with your infra team to configure burst capacity or dedicated pool for the run.
[05:10] Maya: Auth for the benchmark — we'll use service account keys?
[05:14] Samir: Yes, use service accounts with limited scope and short TTL; we'll show how to create one in the console or via API.
[05:20] Priya: SAML/SSO — provisioning engineers into Redwood console. Is user provisioning SCIM available?
[05:24] Samir: Yes we support SCIM for SSO provisioning; SAML for SSO and RBAC with roles. We'll share the SAAS integration doc.
[05:32] [05:32] Avery: quick note on dedicated vs hosted cost — dedicated gives predictable unit economics; hosted is simpler to start. We'll send a pricing sheet after this call.
[05:43] Samir: A few gotchas in SDKs: 1) make sure you pin model versions not just model names to avoid silent regressions, 2) enable prefix KV caching for conversational flows to save tokens, 3) watch for sequence length when batching.
[05:58] Samir: On model pinning: use model_version: 'redwood-2-small-v1.4' rather than 'redwood-2-small'. The SDK supports specifying a fallback_model param for graceful downgrades.
[06:10] Maya: Developer ergonomics — do you have typed clients or swagger?
[06:14] Samir: TS SDK is fully typed; Python has typed stubs and a small CLI. There's also an OpenAPI spec in the repo.
[06:22] Liam: How do we mock the SDK in unit tests?
[06:25] Samir: We provide a local mock server and test helpers in the quickstarts: a small docker-compose dev mock that returns canned responses. For CI you can stub the client methods.
[06:34] Maya: Can you show the sample .env and recommended secrets config?
[06:37] Samir: Sure — recommended .env: 
    REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx
    REDWOOD_REGION=us-east-1
    REDWOOD_ENV=hosted
    REDWOOD_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID=srv-abc

[06:52] Samir: For private installs you may set REDWOOD_PRIVATE_ENDPOINT=https://inference.yourcorp.internal and the SDK will use that instead of the hosted API.
[06:59] Priya: For audit logs — do you provide token-level call traces? We need retention for 12 months for PCI review.
[07:05] Samir: Audit logs with token-level metadata are available for enterprise and can be routed to your SIEM or S3. Retention policies are configurable for dedicated and private. We'll share the compliance options doc.
[07:18] Maya: Any sample config for streaming in Node?
[07:21] Samir: Example: 
    const stream = client.text.stream({model:'redwood-2-large', input: '...'});
    stream.on('data', (chunk) => handleChunk(chunk));
    stream.on('error', (err) => retryHandler(err));

[07:38] [07:38] Samir: Oh — note about batching: server-side batching happens automatically but you can enable client-side batching for microservices that aggregate requests to reduce cost. We include a batching helper in the TS SDK.
[07:51] Liam: For the POC we probably want a small integration first: auth, a basic generation endpoint, and an embedding flow.
[07:57] Maya: Agreed. Timeline: 2 weeks for POC incl. benchmark.
[08:02] Samir: We'll propose this plan: week 0 - setup and keys, run small smoke tests; week 1 - integration and benchmark with Redwood assistance; week 2 - evaluation and next steps.
[08:12] Avery: Next steps recap — we'll send the quickstart repo, security docs (SOC2, encryption, KMS), pricing and dedicated capacity options, and schedule the benchmark run.
[08:22] Maya: Great. Priya — any remaining security blockers?
[08:25] Priya: I'd like the SOC2 and specifics on key management and retention; also a diagram of network flows for our security review.
[08:31] Samir: We'll attach those docs. Also note we can run a private deployment for full network isolation if required.
[08:39] [08:39] Avery: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items discussed.

End of transcript.
